title: Eleven Thousand Neighbors Served: Love Thy City Volunteers Are Building the Next Day of Help
thumbnailMessage: East Texas volunteers are preparing to serve again
summary: Love Thy City says its 2025 gathering served 11,000 people with 600 volunteers. The Tyler nonprofit is now organizing another day of practical assistance and community connection for Aug. 22.
content:
A week before thousands of East Texans are expected to walk into Tyler’s W.T. Brookshire Center looking for help, hundreds of volunteers are doing the quieter work that makes a large service day possible: training, sorting supplies, coordinating partners and preparing to welcome families with dignity.

Love Thy City of East Texas has scheduled its third annual Love Thy City Day for Saturday, Aug. 22. The faith-based nonprofit describes the event as a single place for practical assistance, emotional support, community resources and spiritual connection. Its public materials invite residents to attend, volunteer or sponsor the work.

The scale is significant. In May, Love Thy City’s director of volunteer mobilization told KLTV that the 2025 event drew 11,000 attendees and 600 volunteers. In April, founder and CEO DeMarcus Pierson said 11,000 people were served last year. Those figures are the organization’s reported totals, carried by established local reporting; they should not be inflated into claims about long-term outcomes that have not been independently measured.

What can be verified is the breadth of the effort. Love Thy City says its practical assistance has included student shoe vouchers, electricity vouchers, mother-and-baby bundles, hygiene packages, window air-conditioning units, food-truck vouchers and connections to mental-health services. KLTV reported that the organization has provided electricity assistance, cooling units and household supplies directly to East Texas families.

That work matters because a small household shortfall can become a safety problem. A missing air conditioner during an East Texas summer is not cosmetic. A backpack or shoe expense can collide with a utility bill. A family that does not know which nonprofit handles a specific need can lose days moving between offices. A well-run resource event can reduce that friction by putting providers and volunteers in one place.

The people making those connections are the heart of this story. Love Thy City honored Donnie and Glinda Howard as its Volunteers of the Year in April. They told KLTV that helping even one person improve their quality of life gave the work meaning. Their recognition represents a larger corps of volunteers who return, train and take assigned roles rather than treating service as a photo opportunity.

The nonprofit says training is mandatory for those who want to serve at the Aug. 22 event. That is a responsible standard. Volunteers who may handle family information, distribute limited supplies or direct residents to sensitive services need clear boundaries, accurate instructions and a chain of responsibility. Enthusiasm is valuable; preparation protects the people being helped.

Love Thy City is openly Christian. Its mission statement speaks about expressing love for God and neighbors, and its programming includes spiritual support alongside tangible assistance. Residents should be able to see that identity plainly while also receiving an accurate description of the practical resources on offer. The organization says its goal is to unite churches, businesses, nonprofits and volunteers around work that no single partner could accomplish alone.

Public nonprofit records add another layer of verification. Cause IQ identifies Love Thy City of East Texas as a Tyler-based 501(c)(3) formed in 2024 under EIN 99-1646471 and reports 2024 revenue and expense data from the organization’s tax filing. A fundraising profile on Mightycause lists the same tax ID and describes the planned 2026 assistance. Donors should still review current filings, program details and giving terms before contributing, as they should with any charity.

The group’s rapid growth creates an accountability challenge as well as an opportunity. A crowd measured in thousands needs a public plan for capacity, traffic, accessibility, emergency response, supply limits and follow-up. The organization should explain which resources are guaranteed, which are first-come, which require eligibility screening and how residents’ personal information will be protected. Clear expectations prevent a hopeful family from making a trip for a benefit that has already run out.

Impact reporting should continue after the doors close. The strongest scorecard would separate attendance from households served, list the number and type of benefits distributed, identify how many people were referred to ongoing programs and report what remained unmet. Volunteer hours and partner participation are useful, but the central question is whether families received the help advertised.

The 2024 tax-filing summary and local reports show that Love Thy City is no longer merely an idea. It has mobilized churches, businesses, volunteers and service providers on a scale unusual for a young nonprofit. Last year’s reported 600 volunteers are the clearest evidence of a community choosing coordinated work over isolated good intentions.

Residents who want to participate should use the organization’s current registration and volunteer pages, not an old flyer from the 2025 event. Love Thy City lists the Aug. 22 gathering at the W.T. Brookshire Center and says volunteer orientation is required. People seeking a specific benefit should confirm availability directly before traveling.

The heroism here is collective and practical. It is the volunteer who completes training, the partner who brings a service to one room, the donor who provides a useful item without demanding attention and the organizer who makes sure help reaches a neighbor respectfully. Love Thy City’s next test is to turn that goodwill into a safe, transparent and measurable day of service. East Texas has already shown it can fill the room; the work now is to make every connection count.
